hints: Look at the two types of test separately, carbonates with acid behave very differently from chlorides with alkali.
Remember that all carbonates react with dilute acid to release bubbles of gas, so check what happens in the first and third columns.
For the NaOH tests, think about solubility: magnesium hydroxide is insoluble but barium hydroxide is soluble, so only one of them can form a precipitate.
walkthrough:
**Carbonates plus dilute acid**

Think acid plus carbonate. This is a classic test for carbonate.

$$\text{CO}_3^{2-} + 2\text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Apply to both BaCO3 and MgCO3**

Both are Group 2 carbonates, so both react the same way with $\text{HCl(aq)}$.

$$\text{BaCO}_3\text{(s)} + 2\text{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \text{BaCl}_2\text{(aq)} + \text{CO}_2\text{(g)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$$

**Chlorides plus NaOH, think hydroxide solubility**

Adding $\text{OH}^-$ tests if $\text{M(OH)}_2$ is insoluble. Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group.

Magnesium hydroxide is insoluble, barium hydroxide is soluble in dilute solution.

**Apply to BaCl2 and MgCl2**

For barium, no precipitate forms because $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ stays in solution.

For magnesium, a white precipitate forms:
$$\text{Mg}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{OH}^-\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2\text{(s, white ppt)}$$

options.A: Incorrect. It predicts no change with acid, but both BaCO3 and MgCO3 react with HCl to give effervescence of CO2. It also wrongly swaps the hydroxide results.
options.B: Half right but incomplete. It correctly gives effervescence for both carbonates and no change for BaCl2, but it misses the white precipitate of Mg(OH)2 with MgCl2.
options.C: Correct and reassuring. Both carbonates give effervescence with HCl. BaCl2 gives no change because Ba(OH)2 is soluble, while MgCl2 gives a white ppt because Mg(OH)2 is insoluble. This matches Group 2 trends perfectly.
options.D: Incorrect. It correctly gives effervescence and the Mg(OH)2 white ppt, but it wrongly predicts a white ppt for BaCl2 + NaOH. Students choosing this forget that Ba(OH)2 is soluble, so no precipitate forms in dilute solution.
